summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with suprapubic pain and a history of chronic indwelling Foley catheter use due to hypotonic bladder. He had recently undergone a catheter change due to poor drainage and developed severe lower abdominal pain two days prior to presentation. Initial concern was for a symptomatic UTI given his history of multidrug-resistant organisms, including ESBL-producing E. coli. He was started on intravenous Zosyn and admitted for monitoring. However, after evaluation by Infectious Disease and urology, his symptoms were attributed to catheter-induced bladder irritation rather than active infection. The antibiotics were discontinued, and he was managed conservatively. A yeast infection of the penis was identified and treated with topical antifungal cream. The patient was discharged home with home services, continuing his baseline medications and a bowel regimen, with instructions to secure his catheter bag properly and follow up with urology to discuss long-term management options, including a possible suprapubic catheter.
